title: Conflict resolution
exam_coverage_note: Area C (LOs 10-15) accounts for 20-25% of exam marks, the largest single area.
apm_learning_objective: Understand conflict resolution as the ability to identify and address differences between individuals and/or interest groups.
learning_outcomes: 11a) Know the sources of conflict within a project.
11b) Understand that conflict can have both positive and negative impacts within a project.
11c) Know ways in which conflict can be addressed in different situations (such as Thomas Kilmann Conflict Mode Instrument).
where_this_fits: The counterintuitive LO. Most people arrive believing conflict is a problem to eliminate; the syllabus wants you to understand that too little conflict is more dangerous than too much. It shares content directly with LO5, because negotiation, BATNA and ZOPA sit in this chapter of the source, and it picks up where LO10's engagement stops working. The distinction everything rests on: it is not conflict that is negative or positive, it is how the conflict is conducted.

key_definitions.apm_definition: A difference in ideas, interests, priorities or perceptions. In project-based working it can arise over what to do and how to do it.
key_definitions.plain_english: People wanting different things, or seeing the same thing differently. Normal, and not automatically a problem.

key_definitions.apm_definition: Respectful disagreement: considered, respectful and well facilitated. Necessary to find optimal solutions and make robust decisions.
key_definitions.plain_english: Argument about the issue, conducted properly. The thing that stops a bad idea getting through unchallenged.

key_definitions.apm_definition: Conflict that is acrimonious, disrespectful and poorly managed, arising when emotions overcome reason.
key_definitions.plain_english: Argument that has stopped being about the issue and started being about the people.

key_definitions.apm_definition: What happens when people find disagreement uncomfortable, so the group seeks consensus before it should, rejecting dissenting voices, or prompting people to self-censor contrary views.
key_definitions.plain_english: Agreement reached too early because disagreeing felt awkward. Decisions then rest on 'what we all know'.

key_definitions.apm_definition: The phenomenon whereby groups endorse higher-risk decisions than individuals would, resulting from the confidence produced by a lack of dissent.
key_definitions.plain_english: A group talks itself into a bolder decision than any of its members would have made alone, because nobody objected.

key_definitions.apm_definition: A series of rising steps moving from accord to disagreement, then irritation, anger, abuse and even violence.
key_definitions.plain_english: The ladder conflict climbs when nobody intervenes. The point is that it has recognisable rungs, so it can be caught early.

key_definitions.apm_definition: The desire to achieve our own objectives. A more assertive strategy arises from giving high priority to the outcome.
key_definitions.plain_english: How hard you push for what you want. High when the result matters more than the relationship.

key_definitions.apm_definition: The desire to support others' objectives. A more cooperative strategy arises from giving high priority to the relationship.
key_definitions.plain_english: How much you accommodate what they want. High when the relationship matters more than this particular result.

key_definitions.apm_definition: Someone who helps protagonists to communicate.
key_definitions.plain_english: A third party who improves the conversation. They do not decide the outcome.

key_definitions.apm_definition: Someone who judges the situation and makes a decision.
key_definitions.plain_english: A third party who does decide. The difference from a mediator is the whole point.

core_content.outcome_title: Sources of conflict within a project
core_content.body_markdown:
## The definition, which contains the sources

Conflict is what happens when ideas, interests, priorities or perceptions diverge. Those four are worth learning as a set, because they are already a list of sources: people disagree about what they think, what they want, what they consider most important, and what they believe they are seeing.

Inside a project it shows up in two places: the what, and the how.

## The three areas conflict comes from

| Source | What it looks like |
|---|---|
| What to do | Differing opinions about the right course of action: scope, priorities, solutions |
| Processes to follow | Disagreement about method, governance, ways of working |
| Relationships | Conflict between people rather than about the work |

The source adds that conflict often comes from opinions that differ, or interests that genuinely oppose each other, held by people who care, and not easily reconciled. Both halves are load-bearing: people only fight about things they care about, and genuinely competing interests do not dissolve because everyone is being reasonable.

## Why project work generates it structurally

Worth knowing for scenario questions, drawing on LO10:

- Project professionals rarely hold positional power over the people they need things from.
- Project-based work spans multiple organisations, conflicting priorities and different cultural norms.
- Behaviour itself adds complexity. Power struggles, misaligned communication and conflict are named as sources of complexity in their own right.
- Organisational politics mixes personal and project objectives, creating explicit and hidden agendas, alliances and conflicts.
- Temporary structures sit inside permanent ones, producing competing direction from different managers. That is the matrix problem from LO2.

## How ordinary conflict turns negative

This is the most useful mechanism in 11a. Negative conflict arises when emotions overcome reason.

The source is careful about why that happens: often it is precisely because the people involved care. Strength of feeling is not the fault. The failure point is specific. Things go wrong once the argument stops being between positions and becomes between people. The moment it gets personal, acrimony follows.

So the diagnostic question in any scenario is not 'how heated is this?' but 'is this still about the issue, or is it now about the person?'

## Spotting escalation early

Conflict escalation is a series of rising steps: accord → disagreement → irritation → anger → abuse → and even violence.

Because it has steps, it can be caught. The signs show in body language and voice:

| Signal | What to watch |
|---|---|
| Posture | Which way the body angles: forward is aggressive, away is aversive |
| Gesture | Either aggressive, or self-soothing |
| Face | The mouth, the nostrils, the eyes, the brow |
| Physiology | Changes in breathing, flushing of the skin, pupils widening |
| Voice | Its tone |
| Language | The words being reached for |

The point of the list is not observation for its own sake. Project professionals need the skills to spot the signs of rising negative conflict and defuse it, while keeping the important issues under respectful discussion.

## Preventing it: environment before technique

Avoiding negative conflict begins by building somewhere people can challenge each other and stay respectful. That is an inclusive culture in which:

- people respect one another
- landing on the best solution counts for more than personally being right
- turning out to be wrong is not treated as failing

That second and third point are the real safeguards. Where being wrong carries a cost, people defend positions instead of examining them, and disagreement becomes personal because status is at stake.

exam_tips.heading: How ordinary conflict turns negative
exam_tips.tip: A scenario where two leads raise their voices over a design decision is not automatically negative conflict. Look for the sentence where it stops being about the design and starts being about the person, and quote that moment back in your answer. Emotion alone earns you nothing.

exam_tips.heading: Spotting escalation early
exam_tips.tip: You will not be asked to list six signals for six marks. You will be asked what you noticed and what you did next, so give one or two signals and then the intervention that followed.

exam_tips.heading: Why project work generates it structurally
exam_tips.tip: Where a question asks why a project generated conflict, the marks sit in the structure rather than the personalities. No positional power, multiple organisations, competing priorities, hidden agendas, two managers giving direction. Name two of those and you have a better answer than one that blames a difficult stakeholder.

core_content.outcome_title: Positive and negative impacts of conflict
core_content.body_markdown:
## Three states, not two

The comparison is not conflict versus harmony. It is three states:

| State | Character | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| Negative conflict | Acrimonious, disrespectful, poorly managed. Elevated emotional effect | Drives performance down |
| Positive conflict | Considered, respectful, well facilitated. Measured responses | Drives performance up |
| No conflict | Comfort that is not real. Consensus reached too early, appetite for risk quietly rising, ideas and feelings going unsaid | Creates additional risk |

However, the instinct that conflict is bad and harmony is good is wrong. When somebody puts forward a weak or mistaken idea, hearing an alternative is a gain, not an inconvenience. Conflict becomes disruptive through how it is conducted, never through the mere fact of it.

## Why positive conflict is necessary

It is not merely tolerable: it is necessary. It is how project professionals find optimal solutions and make robust decisions. A respectfully conducted disagreement is the mechanism that challenges thinking, finds better solutions and produces good decisions.

Without it, the cost is stated plainly: the mildest consequence is a better outcome going unfound; the worst is real risk being manufactured across projects, programmes and portfolios.

## What happens when conflict is absent

### Groupthink

Disagreeing feels uncomfortable, so agreement gets reached earlier than the evidence justifies. As the group closes on consensus it starts pushing back on anyone dissenting, or people keep contrary views to themselves.

The consequence: decisions are based on 'what we all know'. Nobody feels able to push against the settled view, so new information and ideas that bear on it never get properly examined. The group is not deciding on the evidence; it is deciding on the portion of the evidence that felt comfortable to raise.

### Risky shift

The second-order effect, and a term worth knowing precisely: a group will back a riskier decision than any of its members would have taken alone. The cause is the false confidence that silence manufactures.

Read that carefully. Silence is being interpreted as agreement, agreement is being read as confidence, and confidence is licensing more risk than any individual would have accepted alone. That is why lack of conflict is dangerous.

## The impacts of negative conflict

When conflict is not conducted constructively:

- Performance drops.
- If it becomes acrimonious, relationship damage must be attended to, otherwise it contaminates morale, motivation and trust across the project team and the stakeholder group.
- Leaving it alone exposes the project, programme or portfolio. Morale suffers, relationships turn poisonous, and confidence drains away.

The word 'contaminate' is well chosen: unaddressed relationship damage does not stay where it started.

## Getting the benefit without the cost

Creating positive conflict rather than either of the failure states needs facilitation skill. Project professionals should allow:

- everyone a turn, so the loudest personalities do not take the room
- all the evidence and every idea to be weighed by the group
- ideas and evidence to be challenged constructively
- dissent to be treated with respect
- enough time to reach outcomes people can act on

The first and fourth are the direct antidotes to groupthink. A dominant personality and an unwelcome dissenter produce the same outcome: a decision made on partial information.

And the honest caveat: a respectful culture and skilled facilitation still will not prevent negative conflict arising anyway. Prevention reduces it; it does not remove the need to handle it.

diagrams.caption: Negative conflict, positive conflict and no conflict
diagrams.heading: Three states, not two
diagrams.spec: Three panels side by side, with an implied performance axis. Negative conflict: acrimonious, disrespectful, poorly managed, elevated emotional effect — arrow pointing down, 'drives performance down'. Positive conflict: considered, respectful, well facilitated, measured responses — arrow pointing up, 'drives performance up'. No conflict: fake comfort, groupthink, risky shift, suppressed ideas and feelings — 'creates additional risk'. The crucial design point is that 'no conflict' must not look like the safe middle option; it needs to read as its own failure state.
diagrams.alt: Three states compared — negative conflict driving performance down, positive conflict driving it up, and no conflict producing fake comfort, groupthink and risky shift that create additional risk.

exam_tips.heading: Three states, not two
exam_tips.tip: The most examinable idea in LO11, and the one that catches people out. Any question offering a choice between conflict and harmony is offering two of three options. Write the third state in, because no conflict creates additional risk and that sentence is often what lifts an answer.

exam_tips.heading: What happens when conflict is absent
exam_tips.tip: Groupthink and risky shift get confused, and a scenario can hand you either. Groupthink is the consensus reached too early; risky shift is the bolder decision that comes out of it. Use both names and show the link between them.

exam_tips.heading: Getting the benefit without the cost
exam_tips.tip: If the scenario asks how you would run the session, answer with what you allow rather than what you ban. Everyone a turn, all the evidence weighed, challenge welcomed, dissent respected, enough time to reach something people can act on.

worked_examples.situation: Your cladding design review runs 20 minutes, every attendee backs the same option, and the sponsor calls it the smoothest meeting of the year.
worked_examples.answer: No. Fast agreement with nothing challenged is the third state, and it creates additional risk. Silence gets read as confidence, so the group backs a bolder option than any member would alone. Ask who disagreed before you sign it off.

core_content.body_markdown:
## Two objectives when intervening

The job is to make room for positive conflict. Once conflict turns negative, stepping in is an obligation, not an option. Managing it has two objectives, and both are needed:

| Objective | Note |
|---|---|
| Reach an outcome that is fair and serves the stakeholders | One party may well end up less happy. Fair and mutually satisfying are not the same thing |
| Address relationship damage to the conflicting parties | Skip this and the damage contaminates morale, motivation and trust |

Resolving the issue while leaving the relationship broken stores up the next conflict.

## The resolution sequence

Resolution can begin when a third party intervenes, or when a participant becomes aware of a damaging dynamic.

| Step | What happens |
|---|---|
| 1. Choose to engage positively | Demonstrating respect to everyone involved. Resolution starts as a decision |
| 2. Build rapport | Without it, the parties will not listen to or understand each other. This step cannot be skipped to save time |
| 3. Share | Facts, definitions, perspectives, concerns and feelings, which only becomes possible once rapport exists |
| 4. Agree criteria for a satisfactory resolution | Each party sets out requirements and preferred outcomes |
| 5. Explore options | Continue until agreement is reached |

The ordering is the lesson: criteria for a good outcome are agreed before options are explored. Reversing those two turns resolution into a negotiation over positions rather than needs.

## The five conflict strategies

The syllabus names the Thomas-Kilmann Conflict Mode Instrument. The model describes conflict on two dimensions:

| Dimension | What it measures | High when |
|---|---|---|
| Assertiveness | Desire to achieve our own objectives | The outcome is the priority |
| Cooperativeness | Desire to support others' objectives | The relationship is the priority |

That mapping, assertiveness to outcome and cooperativeness to relationship, is what makes the model usable in a scenario. Decide which of the two matters more here, and the strategy follows.

| Strategy | Assertive | Cooperative | Use when |
|---|---|---|---|
| Compete | High | Low | The outcome dominates and the relationship is secondary |
| Accommodate | Low | High | The relationship dominates and the outcome is secondary |
| Avoid | Low | Low | Neither outcome nor relationship is important, and some conflicts are not worth pursuing |
| Compromise | Medium | Medium | The easier strategy. Both give up something to create a fair balance |
| Collaborate | High | High | Both matter. Both parties put more into the discussion, creating mutual benefit and enhancing the relationship, a win-win |

Two points the source makes that most summaries drop:

- Avoiding is a legitimate strategy, not a failure of nerve, where neither the outcome nor the relationship is worth the cost.
- Collaboration takes a lot of work and needs a lot of facilitation skill. Crucially, the investment is not always appropriate. Win-win is the best outcome, not the default answer, and recommending collaboration for a trivial dispute is the wrong call.

## Other skills conflict management needs

| Skill | What it is |
|---|---|
| Assertiveness | Holding a line for your principles, the project, your team, yourself |
| Listening | And genuinely understanding what you heard |
| Communicating | Not only ideas, but emotions and perceptions too |
| Resilience | Staying resourceful when under pressure |

## When someone else has to resolve it

Sometimes someone outside has to step in: the sponsor, a stakeholder, or a mediator or arbitrator brought in from outside.

| Role | What they do |
|---|---|
| Mediator | Helps the protagonists communicate. Does not decide |
| Arbitrator | Weighs it up and rules on it |

Set the escalation protocol in advance, up to project governance, then onward to programme or portfolio level. Where the dispute is contractual, the organisation may end up in litigation, or using alternative dispute resolution.

And the balanced position to take: a resolution the parties agree to, meeting stakeholders' requirements where that is achievable, always beats an imposed one. It is still worth naming a final arbiter up front in case a final decision becomes necessary. Naming the arbiter before the dispute is exactly the same principle as LO2's escalation routes. You design the route before you need it.

## Negotiation is a form of conflict

Worth connecting explicitly, because the source treats it as part of this chapter and LO5 examines it. Negotiation follows a process and is conducted with respect, which fits the definition of positive conflict. The five conflict strategies apply to the bargaining step, where 'driving a hard bargain' is the competing mode and does not build sustainable relationships.

So the same two-dimensional judgement applies: how much does this outcome matter, and how much does this relationship matter afterwards?

## When to call for specialists

Where the stakes are high, specialist training in conflict and negotiation exists, and the right move may be to bring in a trained mediator or arbitrator, a procurement specialist, or a lawyer. Recognising the limit of your own competence is part of managing conflict well.

worked_examples.heading: The five conflict strategies
worked_examples.situation: Two engineers have argued for a week over the font on the site signage. The client has not asked, the signs go up Friday, and the two work in different teams afterwards.
worked_examples.ask: Do you run a collaborative session?
worked_examples.answer: No, you avoid. Neither the outcome nor the relationship carries real cost here, and collaboration would spend facilitation effort you need on the cladding dispute instead. Avoiding is legitimate when the conflict is not worth pursuing.

worked_examples.heading: Two objectives when intervening
worked_examples.row_label: Address relationship damage to the conflicting parties
worked_examples.situation: You settle a scope dispute between your commercial lead and the supplier's project manager. The variation lands at £18k and the programme holds.
worked_examples.answer: No. You have met one objective of two. Leave the relationship damaged and it contaminates morale and trust for the remaining nine months of the contract, so book the conversation that repairs it.

misconceptions.wrong: Conflict on a project is a problem to be eliminated.
misconceptions.right: Positive conflict is necessary to find optimal solutions and make robust decisions. What makes conflict disruptive is how it happens, not that it happened.

misconceptions.wrong: A team with no conflict is a healthy team.
misconceptions.right: No conflict is its own failure state: fake comfort, groupthink, risky shift and suppressed ideas, all of which create additional risk. Lack of conflict is dangerous.
It means the group sought consensus before it should, because disagreement felt uncomfortable. Dissenting voices get rejected or people self-censor, so relevant information is never explored.

misconceptions.wrong: Groups make more cautious decisions than individuals.
misconceptions.right: Risky shift describes the opposite. A group will back a riskier decision than any member would alone, because silence gets misread as confidence.

misconceptions.wrong: Conflict turns negative when people get emotional.
misconceptions.right: Emotion often reflects that people care about the issue. It turns negative when it escalates from being about issues to being about people. As soon as it is personalised, acrimony starts.

misconceptions.wrong: Collaboration and win-win is always the right strategy.
misconceptions.right: Collaboration takes a lot of work and facilitation skill, and the investment is not always appropriate. Where neither outcome nor relationship matters much, avoiding is legitimate.

misconceptions.wrong: Avoiding a conflict is always weakness.
misconceptions.right: Some conflicts, where neither the outcome nor the relationship is important, are not worth pursuing. Avoiding is one of the five recognised strategies.

misconceptions.wrong: Resolving the issue resolves the conflict.
misconceptions.right: Managing negative conflict has two objectives: finding a fair outcome, and addressing relationship damage. Unaddressed damage contaminates morale, motivation and trust across the team and stakeholder group.

misconceptions.wrong: A mediator decides who is right.
misconceptions.right: A mediator helps the protagonists communicate. An arbitrator weighs it up and rules on it. Only one of the two actually decides anything.

misconceptions.wrong: A fair resolution leaves both parties content.
misconceptions.right: A fair outcome serves the stakeholders, and this may mean one party is less content. Fairness is measured against the stakeholders' interests, not against equal satisfaction.

memory_aids.acronym: Negative down, positive up, none risky
memory_aids.expansion: The three states and their effects. Negative conflict drives performance down, positive conflict drives it up, and no conflict creates additional risk through groupthink and risky shift.
The diagnostic question for whether conflict has turned negative. Emotion is fine; personalisation is the failure point, because acrimony starts the moment it stops being about the issue.

memory_aids.acronym: Assertive is my outcome, cooperative is your relationship
memory_aids.expansion: The two axes of the five-strategy model. Decide which of outcome and relationship matters more here, and the strategy follows from that.
The resolution sequence: engage, build rapport, share, agree criteria, explore options. Without rapport the parties will not listen, so the later steps cannot work.
A mediator helps the protagonists communicate. An arbitrator judges and makes the decision.

progress_checkpoint: I can define conflict, name the four things it is a difference in, and give the three areas within a project it arises from.
I can explain how conflict turns negative, and identify personalisation rather than emotion as the failure point.
I can describe conflict escalation as a series of steps and name the signals that indicate it is rising.
I can compare negative conflict, positive conflict and no conflict, and state the effect each has on performance.
I can explain groupthink and risky shift, and say why a lack of conflict creates additional risk.
I can name the two objectives of managing negative conflict and explain why addressing relationship damage is not optional.
I can give the resolution sequence in order and explain why rapport must come before exploring options.
I can name the five conflict strategies, place them on assertiveness and cooperativeness, say when each applies, and distinguish a mediator from an arbitrator.
